## Objectives {#objectifs}

This module is the last one of the curriculum. It brings together the physics of the previous modules (zero divergence, symmetries, energy budgets, invariant measures) and the generative models of Module 7 (diffusion, flow matching) to answer the central question of the internship: how can a model that generates fields be made to respect a physical law? By the end of the thirty hours of planned work, you will be able to:

1. classify a physical constraint into one of the four classes of the internship (local linear, local nonlinear, symmetry, statistical “in distribution”), say whether it bears on each sample or on the distribution, and choose the appropriate mechanism (architecture, projection, penalty, guidance, tilting of the distribution);
2. build a generator whose outputs are divergence-free by construction (stream function in 2D, vector potential in 3D with a choice of gauge), and prove that an equivariant velocity field transports an invariant base distribution onto an invariant distribution;
3. prove that, if the data live in a linear subspace $S$, the orthogonal component of the optimal flow is exactly $-\mathbf{x}_\perp/(1-t)$, deduce from it the behavior of free generation, of the final projection and of the projected flow, and check it numerically;
4. explain the Jensen gap and why a penalty on the endpoint prediction is unbiased for a linear constraint but biased for a nonlinear one; situate PIDM, DiffusionPDE and the comparison of Genuist et al. (2026);
5. write the conditional velocity field of guided flow matching, implement DPS-type guidance and measure its bias on an example where the posterior distribution is known;
6. prove the stationarity identities $\mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathcal{L}\varphi] = 0$, show that imposing such an identity sample by sample destroys the distribution, and impose the identity by exponential tilting (I-projection) while knowing its limits;
7. evaluate a generator of MHD fields with physical metrics: relative divergence, spectra, helicities, budgets, topology (Betti numbers, persistent homology, magnetic null points);
8. read critically the five papers cited in the internship offer and say what each one brings to the internship.

## Prerequisites {#prerequis}

The starting point is the M1–M2 level reached at the end of the previous modules. You need to be able to handle the divergence, the curl, the Helmholtz–Hodge decomposition and the Leray projection in Fourier space ([Vector calculus and Fourier analysis](../p1-calcul-vectoriel/index.html)), to know the equations of incompressible MHD, their energy budget and the symmetry $\mathbf{B} \to -\mathbf{B}$ ([Electromagnetism, MHD and the dynamo effect](../p3-mhd-dynamo/index.html)), to know what an invariant measure and an infinitesimal generator are ([Dynamical systems, bifurcations and invariant measures](../p4-systemes-dynamiques/index.html)), and to master conditional expectation, the Kullback–Leibler divergence and Wasserstein distances ([Probability, statistics and optimal transport](../p5-probabilites-transport/index.html)).

Above all, the module assumes that the module [Generative models: diffusion and flow matching](../p7-modeles-generatifs/index.html) has been mastered: flow matching (Lipman et al. 2023), linear path $\mathbf{x}_t = (1-t)\mathbf{x}_0 + t\mathbf{x}_1$, conditional flow matching loss, optimal velocity field $v^\star(\mathbf{x}, t) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0 \mid \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{x}]$, sampling with the Euler scheme. On the code side, you need to know how to train a small network with PyTorch ([Deep learning for physics](../p6-apprentissage-profond/index.html)). The module [Fluid mechanics and turbulence](../p2-mecanique-fluides/index.html) is used in Chapter 7 (energy spectra).

Notation: that of the site (`specs/notations.md`). The flow time $t \in [0, 1]$ is **not** a physical time: $t = 0$ is the noise, $t = 1$ the data. The velocity field of the flow $v_\theta$ must not be confused with the physical velocity $\mathbf{u}$.

## 1. Taxonomy of physical constraints {#ch1}

“Enforcing physics” on a generative model can mean very different things. The zero divergence of $\mathbf{B}$ holds for **each** field; the energy budget of a stationary turbulent state holds only **on average**; the symmetry $\mathbf{B} \to -\mathbf{B}$ holds only for the **distribution**. Confusing these cases leads to errors: one can destroy the distribution one is trying to learn by imposing, sample by sample, a constraint that only holds on average. This chapter fixes the vocabulary used throughout the module and in the [report](../../rapport/index.html#taxonomie).

### 1.1 The framework

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Framework of the internship]{.tag}
A discretized physical system is described by a state $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^D$ (for instance the values of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ on a grid, or their Fourier coefficients), which evolves according to

$$
\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} = F_{\boldsymbol\lambda}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}t + \Sigma\,\mathrm{d}W_t,
$$

where $\boldsymbol\lambda$ gathers the control parameters ($Re$, $Rm$, material properties) and where $\Sigma = 0$ in the deterministic case. The data are **snapshots** of a statistically stationary state: their distribution is an invariant measure $\mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda}$ of the dynamics. The conditional generative model produces a distribution $q_\theta(\cdot\mid\boldsymbol\lambda)$, the image of the Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ under the time-1 flow of the equation $\dot{\mathbf{z}} = v_\theta(\mathbf{z}, t, \boldsymbol\lambda)$.
:::

Two objects therefore coexist: a **sample** $\mathbf{x}$ (a field) and a **distribution** ($\mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda}$ or $q_\theta$). A physical constraint can bear on either one.

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Per-sample constraint, distributional constraint]{.tag}
A **per-sample constraint** is a set $\mathcal{C} \subset \mathbb{R}^D$ such that $\mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda}(\mathcal{C}) = 1$: almost every physical field belongs to $\mathcal{C}$. A **distributional constraint** is a property of the measure $\mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda}$ that is not of this form, for instance an equality of expectations $\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda}}[g] = 0$ or an invariance $g_\#\mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda} = \mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda}$, where $g_\#\mu$ denotes the pushforward of $\mu$ by the map $g$.
:::

A per-sample constraint can be checked on a single generated field. A distributional constraint can only be checked on a **set** of generated fields, with a statistical error. This difference determines everything that follows.

### 1.2 The four classes

::: def
[Definition 1.3 — The four classes of constraints]{.tag}
We distinguish four classes, denoted C1 to C4 in the report and in the PhD proposal.

- **C1, local linear**: $\mathbf{x} \in S$ with $S = \ker A$ a linear subspace. Examples: $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0$, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$, homogeneous linear boundary conditions ($\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$ or $\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 0$ on a wall).
- **C2, local nonlinear**: $c(\mathbf{x}) = 0$ with $c$ nonlinear. Examples: residual of a **stationary** PDE (the Darcy equation, a magnetohydrostatic equilibrium), an algebraic constraint such as $|\mathbf{x}| = 1$.
- **C3, symmetry**: $g_\#\mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda} = \mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda}$ for every $g$ in a group $G$. Examples: $\mathbf{B} \to -\mathbf{B}$, the rotation $R_\pi$ of the VKS experiment in exact counter-rotation, $(Q, D, V) \to (-Q, -D, V)$ in the Gissinger model.
- **C4, statistical**: $\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda}}[\mathcal{L}_{\boldsymbol\lambda}\varphi] = 0$ for test functions $\varphi$, where $\mathcal{L}_{\boldsymbol\lambda}$ is the generator of the dynamics (Chapter 6). Example: the mean energy budget of a stationary state, mean injection equal to mean dissipation.

C1 and C2 are per-sample constraints; C3 and C4 are distributional constraints.
:::

One might think that the evolution equations themselves provide a per-sample constraint: “the generated field must satisfy the PDE”. This is not the case for a snapshot of an unsteady dynamics, and the following proposition states it in finite dimension.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.4 — A snapshot does not “satisfy” an evolution PDE]{.tag}
Let $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = F(\mathbf{x})$ with $F$ locally Lipschitz on an open set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^D$. Every point $\mathbf{x}^\ast \in U$ is the state, at a given time, of a solution of the equation. For a snapshot, the residual $\partial_t\mathbf{x} - F(\mathbf{x})$ cannot be computed (the time derivative is not observed), and any quantity of the form $\mathrm{d}\varphi/\mathrm{d}t = \nabla\varphi\cdot F(\mathbf{x})$ is an **identity** computable on the snapshot, not a constraint.

::: proof
By the Cauchy–Lipschitz theorem, the problem $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = F(\mathbf{x})$, $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{x}^\ast$ has a solution on an interval $[0, \tau)$ with $\tau > 0$; $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is its state at time $0$. No property of $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ alone can therefore distinguish a “physical” state from a “non-physical” state in the sense of the evolution equation. If $\varphi$ is differentiable, the chain rule gives $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\varphi(\mathbf{x}(t)) = \nabla\varphi(\mathbf{x})\cdot F(\mathbf{x})$, an expression that depends only on the state. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In practice, the **explicit** per-sample constraints provided by the physical model are therefore those that do not involve time: C1-type conditions (divergence, boundary conditions) and diagnostic relations (for instance the pressure, which is determined by the velocity). One nuance is in order, however. The snapshots of a stationary regime live on the attractor, which has zero Lebesgue measure for a dissipative dynamics (Remark 6.5): “$\mathbf{x}$ belongs to the attractor” is indeed a per-sample constraint in the sense of Definition 1.2. But the equation does not provide it in any computable form; it is up to the data to teach it.

For a PDE, the statement requires care about the function space (regularity, compatibility conditions), but the message is the same: apart from what the data teach, the information that the evolution equation provides about stationary snapshots is **statistical**. It goes through the distribution, and this is the subject of Chapter 6. A stationary PDE (such as the Darcy equation in PIDM), on the contrary, gives a genuine per-sample constraint of class C2, since every solution field satisfies it.

::: ex
[Example 1.5 — What holds for each field and what holds for the distribution in forced MHD]{.tag}
Consider snapshots $(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{B})$ of forced MHD turbulence in a periodic box, at fixed parameters $(Re, Rm)$. Each snapshot satisfies $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0$ and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$ (C1). On each snapshot, one computes the injection $P = \langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{f}\rangle$ and the dissipation $\varepsilon = \nu\langle|\nabla\mathbf{u}|^2\rangle + \eta\langle|\nabla\mathbf{B}|^2\rangle$; the difference $P - \varepsilon = \mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t$ fluctuates from one snapshot to the next and has no reason to vanish. Only the mean vanishes, $\mathbb{E}[P] = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon]$ (C4). Finally, the distribution of the snapshots is invariant under $\mathbf{B} \to -\mathbf{B}$ if the dynamics visits both polarities, but each snapshot has a given polarity (C3).
:::

![Taxonomy of physical constraints used throughout the module (figure from the report). **a**, The four classes: C1 and C2 hold for each sample and call for potentials, a projection, a penalty or guidance; C3 and C4 hold only for the distribution and call for an equivariant velocity field, a stationarity loss or an exponential tilting. **b**, For the energy budget (C4): projecting each sample onto $\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t = 0$ produces a Dirac (zero variance), whereas the distributional correction keeps the samples and changes their weights. ### 1.3 A mechanism for each class

A generative model offers five places to act: the **architecture** (what the network can produce), the **projection** (correcting the state during or after sampling), the **penalty** (a term added to the training loss), the **guidance** (modifying the velocity field at sampling time, without retraining), and the **tilting of the distribution** (reweighting the samples, or training towards a reweighted distribution). The following table summarizes the choices advocated in this module; Chapters 2 to 6 justify them one by one.

| Class | Holds for | Exact mechanism | Approximate mechanism | Chapter |
|---|---|---|---|:---:|
| C1 local linear | each sample | potentials (architecture); orthogonal projection (Leray) | penalty, guidance | 2, 3, 4 |
| C2 local nonlinear | each sample | nonlinear projection (Gauss–Newton, PCFM) | penalty (Jensen gap), guidance | 3, 4, 5 |
| C3 symmetry | the distribution | equivariant velocity field and invariant base distribution | data augmentation | 2 |
| C4 statistical | the distribution | exponential tilting (I-projection) of the generated distribution | stationarity loss during training | 6 |

Two category errors come up often. The first consists in imposing a constraint of class C3 or C4 on each sample: one obtains a distribution concentrated on a set that the true distribution does not charge (Corollary 6.4). The second consists in handling a C1 constraint with a penalty: the violation decreases without vanishing, whereas an exact mechanism exists and costs almost nothing.

The following code illustrates classes C3 and C4 on the simplest possible system: a particle in a double well, subject to noise. The dynamics is symmetric under $x \to -x$; so is its stationary distribution, but each sample has a sign. The stationarity identity $\mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathcal{L}\varphi] = 0$ (proved in Chapter 6) holds on average, whereas $\mathcal{L}\varphi$ fluctuates from one sample to the next.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Noisy double well: dx = F(x) dt + sigma dW, F(x) = x - x^3 (potential V = x^4/4 - x^2/2).
# The dynamics is symmetric (x -> -x); its stationary distribution is mu(x) ∝ exp(-2V/sigma^2).
sigma, dt, nsteps, N = 0.7, 0.01, 4000, 4000
F = lambda x: x - x**3
x = rng.normal(size=N)
for _ in range(nsteps):                       # Euler-Maruyama, 4000 independent particles
    x += F(x) * dt + sigma * np.sqrt(dt) * rng.normal(size=N)

# Generator L phi = F phi' + (sigma^2/2) phi''
L_energie = lambda x: x * F(x) + sigma**2 / 2      # phi = x^2/2 (an "energy")
L_impair = lambda x: F(x)                           # phi = x

# Exact values by quadrature of the stationary density
g = np.linspace(-3, 3, 6001)
p = np.exp(-2 * (g**4 / 4 - g**2 / 2) / sigma**2)
p /= np.trapezoid(p, g)

print("C3 (symmetry)  : each sample has a sign ; fraction x > 0 =", f"{np.mean(x > 0):.3f}")
print("                 mean of x (distribution) =", f"{x.mean():+.3f}", "(exact 0)")
for nom, Lphi in [("phi = x^2/2", L_energie), ("phi = x", L_impair)]:
    v = Lphi(x)
    exact = np.trapezoid(Lphi(g) * p, g)
    print(f"C4 {nom:11s} : E[L phi] = {v.mean():+.3f} ± {v.std() / np.sqrt(N):.3f} (exact {exact:+.1e}),"
          f" per-sample std = {v.std():.3f}, fraction |L phi| < 0.01 : {np.mean(np.abs(v) < 0.01):.3f}")
# output:
# C3 (symmetry)  : each sample has a sign ; fraction x > 0 = 0.499
#                  mean of x (distribution) = -0.001 (exact 0)
# C4 phi = x^2/2 : E[L phi] = -0.009 ± 0.013 (exact +6.9e-18), per-sample std = 0.813, fraction |L phi| < 0.01 : 0.006
# C4 phi = x     : E[L phi] = -0.006 ± 0.010 (exact +2.1e-17), per-sample std = 0.613, fraction |L phi| < 0.01 : 0.014
```

The mean of $\mathcal{L}\varphi$ vanishes up to statistical error (about one standard deviation of the mean), whereas its per-sample standard deviation is 0.6 to 0.8: fewer than 2% of the samples have $|\mathcal{L}\varphi| < 0.01$. A constraint “$\mathcal{L}\varphi(\mathbf{x}) = 0$ for each $\mathbf{x}$” would therefore reject almost all of the true distribution.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 1
:::
- A constraint bears either on each sample ($\mu(\mathcal{C}) = 1$) or on the distribution (expectation, invariance).
- Four classes: C1 local linear and C2 local nonlinear (per sample), C3 symmetry and C4 statistical (in distribution).
- A snapshot of an unsteady dynamics does not “satisfy” the evolution equation: $\mathrm{d}\varphi/\mathrm{d}t$ is a computable identity; only its mean under the stationary distribution is constrained.
- A mechanism for each class: architecture or projection for C1, nonlinear projection or penalty for C2, equivariance for C3, tilting or a distributional loss for C4.
::::

## 2. Hard constraints through the architecture {#ch2}

The safest way to enforce a constraint is to make its violation impossible: if the network can only produce divergence-free fields, or only symmetric distributions, no learning error can break the constraint. This chapter treats the two cases where this is possible and cheap: potentials for C1, equivariance for C3.

### 2.1 Generating potentials

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.1 — Linear constraint by construction]{.tag}
Let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^D$ be a subspace and $\mathcal{C} : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^D$ a map (the “decoder”) such that $\mathrm{Im}\,\mathcal{C} \subset S$. If the model generates $\mathbf{z} \sim q_{\mathbf{z}}$ and then returns $\mathbf{x} = \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{z})$, the generated distribution satisfies $q(S) = 1$, whatever $q_{\mathbf{z}}$, hence whatever the quality of the learning.

::: proof
$q(S) = q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathcal{C}^{-1}(S)) = q_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbb{R}^m) = 1$, since $\mathcal{C}^{-1}(S) = \mathbb{R}^m$ as soon as the image of $\mathcal{C}$ is contained in $S$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The proposition is trivial; all the interest lies in the choice of $\mathcal{C}$. In 2D, the stream function provides the decoder: $\mathbf{u} = \nabla^\perp\psi = (\partial_y\psi, -\partial_x\psi)$ satisfies $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = \partial_x\partial_y\psi - \partial_y\partial_x\psi = 0$ for every twice-differentiable function $\psi$. This is exactly what FunDiff (Wang et al. 2026) does on the Kolmogorov flow: the decoder produces $\psi$, the velocity is obtained by differentiation, and the authors report a “negligible” predicted divergence, against a much larger divergence without this construction (figures only, no numerical value in the text). Likewise, the 2D magnetic field is written $\mathbf{B} = \nabla^\perp a$.

In 3D, the generalization is the vector potential: $\mathbf{B} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A}$ satisfies $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$ for every $\mathbf{A}$. But the map $\mathbf{A} \mapsto \nabla\times\mathbf{A}$ is not injective: $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{A} + \nabla\chi$ give the same $\mathbf{B}$. For a generative model, this redundancy raises an identifiability problem: if the training data are potentials taken in arbitrary gauges, the distribution of $\mathbf{A}$ is not defined by the physics.

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — Coulomb gauge on the torus]{.tag}
On the torus $\mathbb{T}^3 = [0, 2\pi)^3$, a divergence-free, zero-mean field $\mathbf{B}$ admits a vector potential in the **Coulomb gauge**, that is, such that $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A} = 0$ and $\langle\mathbf{A}\rangle = \mathbf{0}$. In Fourier space, for $\mathbf{k} \neq \mathbf{0}$:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathbf{k}} = \frac{i\,\mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}}{|\mathbf{k}|^2}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathbf{0}} = \mathbf{0}.
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — Existence and uniqueness of the Coulomb potential]{.tag}
On the torus, for every square-integrable, divergence-free, zero-mean $\mathbf{B}$, the field $\mathbf{A}$ of Definition 2.2 satisfies $\nabla\times\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{B}$, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A} = 0$, and it is the only zero-mean field with these two properties. Consequently, the map $\mathbf{A} \mapsto \nabla\times\mathbf{A}$ is a bijection from zero-mean Coulomb fields onto zero-mean divergence-free fields, and the distribution of $\mathbf{B}$ determines that of its Coulomb potential.

::: proof
In Fourier space, the curl reads $\widehat{\nabla\times\mathbf{A}}_{\mathbf{k}} = i\mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathbf{k}}$. With the formula of Definition 2.2 and the vector triple product identity,

$$
i\mathbf{k}\times\frac{i\,\mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}}{|\mathbf{k}|^2} = -\frac{\mathbf{k}(\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}) - |\mathbf{k}|^2\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}}{|\mathbf{k}|^2} = \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}},
$$

since $\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} = 0$ (zero divergence). Moreover $\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}) = 0$, hence $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A} = 0$. For uniqueness, if $\mathbf{A}_1$ and $\mathbf{A}_2$ both qualify, their difference $\mathbf{D}$ satisfies $\mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{D}}_{\mathbf{k}} = \mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{D}}_{\mathbf{k}} = 0$ for every $\mathbf{k} \neq \mathbf{0}$: $\hat{\mathbf{D}}_{\mathbf{k}}$ is both collinear with and orthogonal to $\mathbf{k}$, hence zero; and $\hat{\mathbf{D}}_{\mathbf{0}} = \mathbf{0}$ by the zero-mean condition. The bijection follows, and the distribution of the Coulomb potential is the pushforward of the distribution of $\mathbf{B}$ by the continuous linear map $\mathbf{B} \mapsto \mathbf{A}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The mode $\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{0}$ requires particular attention: a uniform field $\mathbf{B}_0$ is divergence-free but is the curl of no periodic field. A generator of periodic potentials therefore cannot produce a mean field; if one is needed (imposed field, large-scale dynamo in a box), it is generated separately, as three additional numbers.

::: note
[Remark 2.4 — Bounded domains]{.tag}
In a bounded domain such as the VKS or DRESDYN cylinder, the vector potential exists under zero-flux conditions through each connected component of the boundary, and uniqueness requires a boundary condition on $\mathbf{A}$ in addition to $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A} = 0$: either $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 0$, or $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{0}$, the latter being possible only if $\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 0$. If the domain is not simply connected, or if its boundary has several components, flux conditions on $\mathbf{A}$ are also needed, which eliminate the harmonic fields (Amrouche, Bernardi, Dauge and Girault 1998; Amrouche and Seloula 2011). The boundary conditions on $\mathbf{B}$ (matching to an exterior potential field, discontinuous permeability) then become conditions on $\mathbf{A}$, and the magnetic helicity $\int\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}$ depends on the gauge if $\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{n} \neq 0$ (Berger and Field 1984). This is one of the obstacles to moving on to realistic dynamos.
:::

::: note
[Remark 2.5 — “Zero divergence” depends on the discrete operator]{.tag}
On a grid, $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{A}) = 0$ is exact only if the discrete divergence and curl are **compatible**: spectral derivatives, or finite differences on a staggered grid (Yee or MAC type). If one computes $\mathbf{B}$ by Fourier and then its divergence by centered differences, one finds a truncation error that has nothing to do with the model. The divergence metric must therefore be computed with the same operator as the one that defines the constraint (Chapter 7).
:::

The following code checks Proposition 2.3 and the two remarks on a random field of $16^3$ points.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

# Torus [0, 2pi)^3 discretized with n^3 points; spectral derivatives, exact on the represented modes.
n = 16
k1 = np.fft.fftfreq(n, d=1.0 / n)
K = np.stack(np.meshgrid(k1, k1, k1, indexing="ij"))            # (3, n, n, n)
k2 = (K**2).sum(0); k2[0, 0, 0] = 1.0
garde = (np.abs(K) < n // 2).all(0)                              # the Nyquist modes are removed
fft, ifft = (lambda f: np.fft.fftn(f, axes=(-3, -2, -1))), (lambda f: np.fft.ifftn(f, axes=(-3, -2, -1)).real)
curl = lambda Ah: np.stack([1j * (K[1] * Ah[2] - K[2] * Ah[1]),
                            1j * (K[2] * Ah[0] - K[0] * Ah[2]),
                            1j * (K[0] * Ah[1] - K[1] * Ah[0])])
div = lambda Fh: (1j * K * Fh).sum(0)

# An "arbitrary" random vector potential (no gauge imposed), k^-2 spectrum
A = ifft(fft(rng.normal(size=(3, n, n, n))) * garde / k2)
Ah = fft(A)
Bh = curl(Ah); B = ifft(Bh)
rel = lambda Fh: np.linalg.norm(div(Fh)) / np.sqrt((k2 * (np.abs(Fh)**2).sum(0)).sum())   # |div| / |grad|
print("relative divergence of B = curl A      :", f"{rel(Bh):.1e}")

# Gauge freedom: A + grad chi gives the same B
chi_h = fft(rng.normal(size=(n, n, n))) * garde / k2
Ah2 = Ah + 1j * K * chi_h
print("max |curl(A + grad chi) - curl A|      :", f"{np.abs(ifft(curl(Ah2)) - B).max():.1e}")

# Coulomb gauge reconstructed from B: A_c = i k x B / |k|^2
Ach = 1j * np.cross(K, Bh, axis=0) / k2
print("relative |div A_c|, max |curl A_c - B| :", f"{rel(Ach):.1e}", f"{np.abs(ifft(curl(Ach)) - B).max():.1e}")

# Magnetic helicity <A.B>: identical in the three gauges (torus, zero-mean B)
H = lambda Ah_: np.mean((ifft(Ah_) * B).sum(0))
print("H_M with A, A + grad chi, A_c          :", f"{H(Ah):.6f} {H(Ah2):.6f} {H(Ach):.6f}")

# Pitfall: measuring the divergence with ANOTHER discrete operator (centered differences)
h = 2 * np.pi / n
dc = lambda f, ax: (np.roll(f, -1, ax) - np.roll(f, 1, ax)) / (2 * h)
div_fd = dc(B[0], 0) + dc(B[1], 1) + dc(B[2], 2)
grad_fd = np.sqrt(sum(dc(B[i], j)**2 for i in range(3) for j in range(3)).mean())
print("relative divergence of B, finite diff. :", f"{np.sqrt((div_fd**2).mean()) / grad_fd:.1e}")
# output:
# relative divergence of B = curl A      : 3.9e-17
# max |curl(A + grad chi) - curl A|      : 1.4e-16
# relative |div A_c|, max |curl A_c - B| : 3.4e-17 1.1e-16
# H_M with A, A + grad chi, A_c          : 0.002351 0.002351 0.002351
# relative divergence of B, finite diff. : 2.2e-01
```

Three results stand out. The divergence of $\nabla\times\mathbf{A}$ vanishes to machine precision, whatever the gauge. The magnetic helicity does not depend on the gauge on the torus (this is proved in Proposition 7.4). On the other hand, the **same** field $\mathbf{B}$, exactly solenoidal in the spectral sense, has a relative “divergence” of 22% if one measures it with centered differences: this number only measures the incompatibility of the two operators, made worse here by the energy present at small scales. The Nyquist modes are removed because the spectral derivative of a Nyquist mode is not defined in a real-valued way.

Other architectures give divergence-free fields without going through an explicit scalar or vector potential. Richter-Powell, Lipman and Chen (2022) build divergence-free networks in any dimension from differential forms (the row-wise divergence of an antisymmetric matrix field vanishes), at a cost quadratic in the dimension; they show that these networks are universal on the torus up to a constant field. For the internship, the vector potential is the most direct route in 3D, and these networks are an alternative when one wants a field defined at every point (functional decoder).

### 2.2 Equivariance and invariant distributions

The symmetry $\mathbf{B} \to -\mathbf{B}$ is a property of the distribution, not of the fields. The right tool is therefore not a constraint on the output, but a constraint on the **transport** that builds the distribution.

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Group action, invariance, equivariance]{.tag}
Let $G$ be a finite group acting on $\mathbb{R}^D$ by linear isometries $\mathbf{x} \mapsto g\mathbf{x}$. A distribution $\mu$ is **$G$-invariant** if $g_\#\mu = \mu$ for every $g \in G$, that is, if $g\mathbf{X}$ has the same distribution as $\mathbf{X}$ when $\mathbf{X} \sim \mu$. A velocity field $v(\mathbf{x}, t)$ is **$G$-equivariant** if $v(g\mathbf{x}, t) = g\,v(\mathbf{x}, t)$ for all $g$, $\mathbf{x}$, $t$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.7 — Symmetries of the internship]{.tag}
(a) In incompressible MHD, if $(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{B})$ is a solution, so is $(\mathbf{u}, -\mathbf{B})$: the Lorentz force $(\nabla\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{B}$ is quadratic in $\mathbf{B}$ and the induction equation is linear in $\mathbf{B}$. The action $g(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{B}) = (\mathbf{u}, -\mathbf{B})$ is a linear isometry of order 2. (b) In the three-mode model of Gissinger (2012), the action is $(Q, D, V) \to (-Q, -D, V)$. (c) In a square periodic box, an isotropically forced turbulence has a distribution invariant under the dihedral group of rotations by $\pi/2$ and reflections, which acts on a vector field by $(g\mathbf{u})(\mathbf{x}) = R\,\mathbf{u}(R^{-1}\mathbf{x})$. (d) In the VKS experiment in exact counter-rotation, the rotation $R_\pi$ by an angle $\pi$ about an axis perpendicular to the axis of the cylinder exchanges the two impellers.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.8 — Equivariant field and invariant base distribution give an invariant distribution]{.tag}
Let $v$ be a $G$-equivariant velocity field, regular enough for the equation $\dot{\mathbf{z}} = v(\mathbf{z}, t)$ to have a unique solution $\Phi_t(\mathbf{z}_0)$ on $[0, 1]$, and $\gamma$ a $G$-invariant base distribution (for instance $\gamma = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, invariant under every linear isometry). Then $q = (\Phi_1)_\#\gamma$ is $G$-invariant.

::: proof
*First proof (uniqueness of solutions).* Fix $g \in G$ and $\mathbf{z}_0$. The curve $\mathbf{y}(t) = g\,\Phi_t(\mathbf{z}_0)$ satisfies $\dot{\mathbf{y}} = g\,v(\Phi_t(\mathbf{z}_0), t) = v(g\Phi_t(\mathbf{z}_0), t) = v(\mathbf{y}, t)$ by equivariance, and $\mathbf{y}(0) = g\mathbf{z}_0$. By uniqueness, $\mathbf{y}(t) = \Phi_t(g\mathbf{z}_0)$: the flow commutes with $g$. Then, for the pushforward measure,

$$
g_\# q = g_\#(\Phi_1)_\#\gamma = (g\circ\Phi_1)_\#\gamma = (\Phi_1\circ g)_\#\gamma = (\Phi_1)_\#(g_\#\gamma) = (\Phi_1)_\#\gamma = q.
$$

*Second proof (continuity equation).* The density $\rho_t$ of $(\Phi_t)_\#\gamma$ solves $\partial_t\rho_t + \nabla\cdot(\rho_t v) = 0$ with $\rho_0 = \gamma$. Set $\tilde\rho_t(\mathbf{x}) = \rho_t(g^{-1}\mathbf{x})$, the density of $g_\#\rho_t$ (the Jacobian of $g$ is $\pm 1$). Since $g$ is orthogonal and $v$ equivariant, a direct computation with the chain rule gives $\nabla\cdot(\tilde\rho_t v)(\mathbf{x}) = [\nabla\cdot(\rho_t v)](../../../prep/p8-contraintes-physiques/g^{-1}\mathbf{x})$; hence $\tilde\rho_t$ solves the same equation with the same initial datum $\tilde\rho_0 = \gamma$. By uniqueness of the solution of the continuity equation (Lipschitz field), $\tilde\rho_t = \rho_t$ for every $t$, in particular at $t = 1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This proposition is a special case of the result of Köhler, Klein and Noé (2020) on equivariant normalizing flows. It says something strong: the invariance of the generated distribution is **exact**, even if the network has learned the distribution poorly, and even if the training data are not symmetric. It remains to build an equivariant field and to check that this costs nothing in accuracy.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.9 — Symmetrization and flow matching loss]{.tag}
For an arbitrary field $v$, the symmetrized field

$$
v_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbf{x}, t) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G} g^{-1}\,v(g\mathbf{x}, t)
$$

is $G$-equivariant. If the data distribution $\mu$ and the base distribution are $G$-invariant, the population flow matching loss $\mathcal{J}(v) = \mathbb{E}\,\|v(\mathbf{x}_t, t) - (\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0)\|^2$ satisfies $\mathcal{J}(v_{\mathrm{sym}}) \le \mathcal{J}(v)$.

::: proof
*Equivariance.* For $h \in G$, the change of index $g' = gh$ gives $v_{\mathrm{sym}}(h\mathbf{x}, t) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g'} h\,g'^{-1}v(g'\mathbf{x}, t) = h\,v_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbf{x}, t)$.

*Loss.* If $\mu$ and $\gamma$ are invariant, the triple $(g\mathbf{x}_0, g\mathbf{x}_1, g\mathbf{x}_t)$ has the same distribution as $(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_t)$ (the coupling is independent and the path is linear). With the isometry $g$, one obtains $\mathcal{J}(g^{-1}v(g\,\cdot)) = \mathbb{E}\|g^{-1}v(g\mathbf{x}_t) - (\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0)\|^2 = \mathbb{E}\|v(g\mathbf{x}_t) - (g\mathbf{x}_1 - g\mathbf{x}_0)\|^2 = \mathcal{J}(v)$. The functional $\mathcal{J}$ is convex in $v$ (square of a norm); by Jensen's inequality applied to the average of the $|G|$ fields $g^{-1}v(g\,\cdot)$, $\mathcal{J}(v_{\mathrm{sym}}) \le \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g\mathcal{J}(g^{-1}v(g\,\cdot)) = \mathcal{J}(v)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The optimal field $v^\star$ is therefore itself equivariant when the data distribution is (it is the unique minimizer of the population loss). Imposing equivariance takes nothing away from the model class: the search is restricted to a set that contains the solution. **Data augmentation** (adding $g\mathbf{x}$ for each $\mathbf{x}$ of the training set) makes the empirical distribution invariant, hence the population minimizer equivariant, but the learned network is only approximately so. For a small finite group such as $\{\mathrm{id}, \mathbf{B} \mapsto -\mathbf{B}\}$, symmetrization costs two evaluations of the network; for the rotations and reflections of a grid, one uses equivariant convolutions (Cohen and Welling 2016).

The following code reproduces, in two dimensions, the situation of the internship: the true distribution is symmetric, but the training set is finite and unbalanced (a simulation of finite duration spent more time in one polarity than in the other). We compare free flow matching with flow matching whose field is antisymmetrized, $v_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbf{x}) = \tfrac12(v(\mathbf{x}) - v(-\mathbf{x}))$.

```python
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(1); torch.manual_seed(0)

# Symmetric true distribution (g: x -> -x, analogue of (Q, D, V) -> (-Q, -D, V)), but a FINITE
# and unbalanced training set: 700 points in the + lobe, 300 in the - lobe.
c = torch.tensor([1.5, 0.8])
data = torch.cat([c + 0.3 * torch.randn(700, 2), -c + 0.3 * torch.randn(300, 2)])

def mlp():
    return torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(3, 64), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 64),
                               torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 2))

def train(net, vfun, steps=1500):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=2e-3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        x1 = data[torch.randint(len(data), (256,))]
        x0, t = torch.randn(256, 2), torch.rand(256, 1)
        xt = (1 - t) * x0 + t * x1
        loss = ((vfun(net, xt, t) - (x1 - x0))**2).sum(1).mean()
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

libre = lambda net, x, t: net(torch.cat([x, t], 1))
equiv = lambda net, x, t: 0.5 * (libre(net, x, t) - libre(net, -x, t))   # v(-x) = -v(x) exactly

@torch.no_grad()
def sample(net, vfun, z, nsteps=100):
    x = z.clone()
    for i in range(nsteps):
        t = torch.full((len(x), 1), i / nsteps)
        x = x + vfun(net, x, t) / nsteps
    return x

z = torch.randn(4000, 2)
for nom, vfun in [("free", libre), ("equivariant", equiv)]:
    net = mlp(); train(net, vfun)
    x, xm = sample(net, vfun, z), sample(net, vfun, -z)
    print(f"{nom:12s}: fraction in the + lobe = {(x[:, 0] > 0).float().mean():.3f},"
          f"  max |Phi(-z) + Phi(z)| = {(x + xm).abs().max():.1e}")
# output:
# free        : fraction in the + lobe = 0.688,  max |Phi(-z) + Phi(z)| = 2.7e+00
# equivariant : fraction in the + lobe = 0.489,  max |Phi(-z) + Phi(z)| = 0.0e+00
```

The free model faithfully reproduces the imbalance of the training set (69% in the positive lobe), which is a sampling artifact. The equivariant model satisfies $\Phi_1(-\mathbf{z}) = -\Phi_1(\mathbf{z})$ exactly (the gap is zero, not merely small, because antisymmetrization is exact in floating-point arithmetic): by drawing the noises in pairs $(\mathbf{z}, -\mathbf{z})$, the fraction would be exactly $1/2$; with 4000 independent draws, one observes $0.489$, 1.4 standard deviations away from $0.5$. This is the mechanism chosen for the symmetry $(Q, D, V) \to (-Q, -D, V)$ in experiment E1 of the internship ([report, E1](../../rapport/index.html#e1)): the stationarity identities of Chapter 6 do not fix the relative weights of two symmetric ergodic components, so the symmetry must be imposed separately.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 2
:::
- A decoder whose image lies in $S$ makes the C1 constraint exact whatever the quality of the learning: $\mathbf{u} = \nabla^\perp\psi$ in 2D, $\mathbf{B} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A}$ in 3D.
- The vector potential is only defined up to a gradient: the Coulomb gauge ($\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathbf{k}} = i\mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}/|\mathbf{k}|^2$) is fixed so that the distribution of $\mathbf{A}$ is well defined; the mean field is generated separately; in a bounded domain, the gauge and the boundary conditions are an obstacle.
- Zero divergence only makes sense with a given discrete operator, compatible with the curl.
- Equivariant velocity field + invariant base distribution ⇒ exactly invariant generated distribution; symmetrization does not degrade the loss when the data are invariant.
::::

## 3. Hard constraints through projection {#ch3}

When one does not want to change the representation (one generates $\mathbf{u}$ or $\mathbf{B}$ directly, for instance because the decoder is imposed or because the geometry makes potentials awkward), one can correct the state by an orthogonal projection onto $S$. The Leray projection, seen in Module 1, is the central example. This chapter answers a precise question: at what point should one project, and why does the choice matter, given that the projection always makes the constraint exact?

### 3.1 The Leray projection

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Orthogonal projection onto solenoidal fields]{.tag}
Let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^D$ be the subspace of divergence-free discrete fields and $P$ the orthogonal projector onto $S$ ($P^2 = P$, $P^{\mathsf{T}} = P$). On the torus, $P$ is the Leray projection, diagonal in Fourier space: for $\mathbf{k} \neq \mathbf{0}$,

$$
\widehat{(P\mathbf{u})}_{\mathbf{k}} = \Big(I - \frac{\mathbf{k}\mathbf{k}^{\mathsf{T}}}{|\mathbf{k}|^2}\Big)\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}},
$$

and the mean mode is kept. We write $\mathbf{x}_\parallel = P\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}_\perp = (I - P)\mathbf{x}$ for the components of $\mathbf{x}$ in $S$ and orthogonal to $S$.
:::

Module 1 proves that $P\mathbf{u}$ is the solenoidal field closest to $\mathbf{u}$ in the $L^2$ norm, that $P$ commutes with derivatives on the torus, and that the projection becomes a global Poisson problem in the presence of walls. Here, only linearity and orthogonality matter.

### 3.2 The optimal flow when the data live in a subspace

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Decomposition of the optimal flow]{.tag}
Assume $\mu(S) = 1$ and $\mathbf{x}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ independent of $\mathbf{x}_1 \sim \mu$, with $\mathbf{x}_t = (1-t)\mathbf{x}_0 + t\mathbf{x}_1$. Then, for $t < 1$, the optimal velocity field of flow matching reads

$$
v^\star(\mathbf{x}, t) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{x}_1 - P\mathbf{x}_0 \,\big|\, P\mathbf{x}_t = P\mathbf{x}\big]}_{=:\,v_S(P\mathbf{x},\,t)\ \in\ S} \; - \; \frac{(I - P)\mathbf{x}}{1 - t}.
$$

The component in $S$ depends only on $P\mathbf{x}$, and the orthogonal component is explicit.

::: proof
Write $\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0 = (\mathbf{x}_1 - P\mathbf{x}_0) - (I - P)\mathbf{x}_0$. Since $\mathbf{x}_1 \in S$ almost surely, $(I - P)\mathbf{x}_t = (1 - t)(I - P)\mathbf{x}_0$: the orthogonal component of the noise is a function of $\mathbf{x}_t$, and $\mathbb{E}[(I-P)\mathbf{x}_0 \mid \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{x}] = (I - P)\mathbf{x}/(1 - t)$. For the other term, the isotropy of the Gaussian noise makes $P\mathbf{x}_0$ and $(I - P)\mathbf{x}_0$ independent (Gaussian vector with covariance $I$, uncorrelated components in a basis adapted to $S \oplus S^\perp$). The triple $(\mathbf{x}_1, P\mathbf{x}_0, P\mathbf{x}_t)$ is therefore independent of $(I - P)\mathbf{x}_t = (1-t)(I-P)\mathbf{x}_0$. Conditioning on $\mathbf{x}_t$ amounts to conditioning on the pair $(P\mathbf{x}_t, (I-P)\mathbf{x}_t)$, and the second coordinate, being independent, can be removed from the conditioning. Finally $\mathbf{x}_1 - P\mathbf{x}_0 \in S$, hence so is its conditional expectation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Corollary 3.3 — Four consequences]{.tag}
Under the assumptions of Proposition 3.2:

(a) with the exact field $v^\star$, the orthogonal component of a trajectory satisfies $\mathbf{x}_\perp(t) = (1 - t)\,\mathbf{x}_\perp(0)$: free generation lands exactly in $S$ at $t = 1$;

(b) the component in $S$ obeys $\dot{\mathbf{x}}_\parallel = v_S(\mathbf{x}_\parallel, t)$, which does not see $\mathbf{x}_\perp$; hence, with $v^\star$, free generation, free generation followed by a final projection, the projected flow (Section 3.3), the flow in $S$ and the generation of potentials give **the same distribution**;

(c) the differences observed between these mechanisms come only from the approximation error of the network and from what it is asked to learn, not from the target;

(d) the orthogonal component of the target, $-\mathbf{x}_\perp/(1 - t)$, is unbounded as $t \to 1$ outside $S$: it is a **stiff** restoring term that the network must represent.

::: proof
(a) The orthogonal component of the equation is $\dot{\mathbf{x}}_\perp = -\mathbf{x}_\perp/(1 - t)$, whose solution is $(1-t)\mathbf{x}_\perp(0)$. (b) Projecting the equation onto $S$ gives $\dot{\mathbf{x}}_\parallel = P v^\star = v_S(\mathbf{x}_\parallel, t)$; the initial distribution of $\mathbf{x}_\parallel(0) = P\mathbf{x}_0$ is $\mathcal{N}(0, P)$ in all cases, and $v_S$ is exactly the optimal field of the flow matching problem posed in $S$ (noise $P\mathbf{x}_0$, data $\mathbf{x}_1$). For potentials, flow matching posed on $\psi$, with its own optimal field, transports the noise onto the distribution of $\psi$, the preimage of $\mu$ under the linear bijection $\psi \mapsto \nabla^\perp\psi$ from the space of (zero-mean) potentials onto $S$; the image of this distribution under the bijection is $\mu$. (c) follows from (b). (d) is immediate. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Consequence (b) is important for reading published results: in the limit of perfect learning, all exact mechanisms are equivalent. What distinguishes them in practice is what the network must learn and what it sees as input. The following proposition specifies what remains of the orthogonal component with an imperfect network and the Euler scheme, the most widely used one.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — Final divergence of a free generation integrated with Euler]{.tag}
Write the orthogonal component of the network as $(I-P)v_\theta(\mathbf{x}, t) = -\mathbf{x}_\perp/(1-t) + \mathbf{e}(\mathbf{x}, t)$, where $\mathbf{e}$ is the error of the network with respect to the target of Proposition 3.2. With the explicit Euler scheme on the grid $t_i = i h$, $h = 1/N$, the final orthogonal component is exactly

$$
\mathbf{x}_\perp^{(N)} = h\,\mathbf{e}\big(\mathbf{x}^{(N-1)}, t_{N-1}\big).
$$

It depends only on the error of the network **at the last step**, at $t = 1 - h$: the errors of the previous steps are erased by the restoring term.

::: proof
The Euler step reads $\mathbf{x}_\perp^{(i+1)} = \mathbf{x}_\perp^{(i)} - h\,\mathbf{x}_\perp^{(i)}/(1 - t_i) + h\,\mathbf{e}_i = \frac{1 - t_{i+1}}{1 - t_i}\,\mathbf{x}_\perp^{(i)} + h\,\mathbf{e}_i$, with $\mathbf{e}_i = \mathbf{e}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, t_i)$. At the last step, $1 - t_N = 0$, hence $\mathbf{x}_\perp^{(N)} = 0\cdot\mathbf{x}_\perp^{(N-1)} + h\,\mathbf{e}_{N-1}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Two practical remarks follow. First, with the exact field ($\mathbf{e} = 0$), the fixed-step Euler scheme solves the orthogonal component exactly, whatever $h$ (the factor telescopes). Second, a second-order scheme of Heun type, or a Runge–Kutta scheme, evaluates the field at $t = 1$ at the last step, where the orthogonal target is infinite outside $S$: these schemes require stopping the integration at $t = 1 - \delta$. But the essential point lies elsewhere: at the last step, the target $-\mathbf{x}_\perp/h$ is a very stiff function of $\mathbf{x}_\perp$, which a network of reasonable size represents poorly; the residual divergence of a free generation measures this difficulty (Exercise 6).

### 3.3 Projected flow and flow in $S$

::: def
[Definition 3.5 — Final projection, projected flow, flow in $S$]{.tag}
With a field $v_\theta$ and the Euler scheme:

- the **final projection** integrates freely from $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, then returns $P\mathbf{x}^{(N)}$;
- the **projected flow** starts from $P\mathbf{z}$ and reprojects after each step: $\mathbf{x}^{(i+1)} = P\big(\mathbf{x}^{(i)} + h\,v_\theta(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, t_i)\big)$;
- the **flow in $S$** uses the projected flow at sampling time **and** a projected noise $P\mathbf{x}_0$ during training: the network is never evaluated outside $S$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.6 — The projected flow stays in $S$]{.tag}
The projected flow stays in $S$ at every step, whatever $v_\theta$. With the exact field $v^\star$, it coincides step by step with the Euler scheme of the flow matching problem posed in $S$, hence it has the same limit distribution as the other mechanisms of Corollary 3.3.

::: proof
Each iterate is the image of a vector under $P$, hence belongs to $S$. If $\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \in S$, then $(I - P)\mathbf{x}^{(i)} = 0$ and, by Proposition 3.2, $P v^\star(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, t_i) = v_S(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, t_i)$; the step reads $\mathbf{x}^{(i+1)} = \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + h\,v_S(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, t_i)$, which is the Euler step of the problem posed in $S$, with the same initial datum $P\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, P)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With a learned network, the projected flow has a defect that the proposition does not see. If $v_\theta$ was trained with a full noise, at $t < 1$ it has only seen inputs whose orthogonal component is $(1-t)\mathbf{x}_\perp(0)$, with a norm of order $(1-t)\sqrt{\dim S^\perp}$. The projected flow evaluates it on inputs with a **zero** orthogonal component: this is a distribution shift, whose effect depends on the network. The flow in $S$ removes this shift, and also removes the stiff term from the target: during training, $\mathbf{x}_1 - P\mathbf{x}_0 \in S$.

The following interactive diagram isolates two typical defects of an imperfect network on an example where $S$ is the horizontal axis of the plane and where the data form two bumps on this axis. The component of the field in $S$ is exact; one can **truncate the stiffness** (the network can only represent $-y/(1-t)$ down to $1 - t = \tau$) and add a **leakage** of the orthogonal component into $S$ (the network adds $\kappa\,y$ to the horizontal velocity).

```{=html}
<label>Leakage κ <input type="range" id="p8f-kap" min="0" max="1.5" step="0.05" value="0.6"> <span id="p8f-kapv">0.60</span></label>
<label>Euler steps N <input type="range" id="p8f-n" min="5" max="200" step="5" value="50"> <span id="p8f-nv">50</span></label>
</div>
<canvas id="p8f-canvas" width="720" height="470" role="img" aria-label="Particle trajectories from a Gaussian noise towards the horizontal axis, then a histogram of the final positions compared with the target distribution; the numerical values are given below the figure."></canvas>
<div class="widget-readout" id="p8f-out" aria-live="polite"></div>
<p class="widget-note">Top: 40 trajectories in the plane, from t = 0 (noise) to t = 1; the horizontal line is the subspace S. Bottom: target distribution on S (curve) and histogram of the final positions projected onto S (2000 particles). With τ = 0 and κ = 0, the field is exact and the three mechanisms give the same distribution (Corollary 3.3). The truncation leaves a final orthogonal component (a “divergence”) that only the projection removes; the leakage distorts the distribution in S, and the final projection does not correct it.</p>
</div>
<script>
(function () {
  var root = document.getElementById("p8w-flot"); if (!root) return;
  var cv = root.querySelector("#p8f-canvas"), mode = root.querySelector("#p8f-mode"),
      tau = root.querySelector("#p8f-tau"), kap = root.querySelector("#p8f-kap"), nst = root.querySelector("#p8f-n"),
      out = root.querySelector("#p8f-out");
  var M = [-1.2, 1.2], s = 0.25, NP = 2000, NT = 40;
  function css(n) { return getComputedStyle(root).getPropertyValue(n).trim() || "#888"; }
  function f2(v) { return v.toFixed(2).replace("-", "−"); }
  function f3(v) { var a = Math.abs(v); if (a !== 0 && a < 1e-3) return v.toExponential(1).replace("e", "·10^"); return v.toFixed(3).replace("-", "−"); }
  // fixed seed: the same noise at every redraw
  var seed = 12345; function rnd() { seed = (seed * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2147483648; return seed / 2147483648; }
  function gauss() { var u = Math.max(rnd(), 1e-12), v = rnd(); return Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * v); }
  var Z = []; for (var i = 0; i < NP; i++) Z.push([gauss(), gauss()]);
  var target = []; for (i = 0; i < NP; i++) target.push(M[i % 2] + s * gauss()); target.sort(function (a, b) { return a - b; });
  function vS(x, t) {            // component in S of the optimal field (1D Gaussian mixture)
    var va = t * t * s * s + (1 - t) * (1 - t), num = 0, den = 0;
    for (var k = 0; k < 2; k++) {
      var w = Math.exp(-(x - t * M[k]) * (x - t * M[k]) / (2 * va));
      num += w * (M[k] + t * s * s / va * (x - t * M[k])); den += w;
    }
    return (num / Math.max(den, 1e-300) - x) / (1 - t);
  }
  function run(keep) {
    var md = mode.value, T = parseFloat(tau.value), K = parseFloat(kap.value), N = parseInt(nst.value, 10), h = 1 / N;
    var fin = [], paths = [], ys = 0;
    for (var p = 0; p < NP; p++) {
      var x = Z[p][0], y = md === "projete" ? 0 : Z[p][1], path = p < keep ? [[x, y]] : null;
      for (var i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        var t = i * h, vx = vS(x, t) + K * y, vy = -y / Math.max(1 - t, T, 1e-12);
        x += h * vx; y += h * vy; if (md === "projete") y = 0;
        if (path) path.push([x, y]);
      }
      if (md === "finale") { if (path) path.push([x, 0]); ys += Math.abs(y); y = 0; } else ys += Math.abs(y);
      fin.push(x); if (path) paths.push(path);
    }
    fin.sort(function (a, b) { return a - b; });
    var w1 = 0; for (p = 0; p < NP; p++) w1 += Math.abs(fin[p] - target[p]); w1 /= NP;
    var yfin = md === "libre" ? ys / NP : 0;
    return { paths: paths, fin: fin, w1: w1, y: yfin, ybefore: ys / NP };
  }
  function draw() {
    root.querySelector("#p8f-tauv").textContent = f2(parseFloat(tau.value));
    root.querySelector("#p8f-kapv").textContent = f2(parseFloat(kap.value));
    root.querySelector("#p8f-nv").textContent = nst.value;
    var dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1, W = cv.clientWidth || 720, H = Math.round(W * 470 / 720);
    cv.width = Math.round(W * dpr); cv.height = Math.round(H * dpr);
    var g = cv.getContext("2d"); g.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0);
    var bg = css("--bg"), ink = css("--ink"), hair = css("--hair"), c1 = css("--p8-c1"), c2 = css("--p8-c2"), gr = css("--p8-g");
    g.fillStyle = bg; g.fillRect(0, 0, W, H);
    var top = 0.66 * H, X = function (x) { return (x + 3) / 6 * W; }, Y = function (y) { return top / 2 - y / 2.6 * (top / 2); };
    g.strokeStyle = hair; g.lineWidth = 1; g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(0, top); g.lineTo(W, top); g.stroke();
    g.strokeStyle = ink; g.lineWidth = 1.5; g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(X(-3), Y(0)); g.lineTo(X(3), Y(0)); g.stroke();
    g.fillStyle = ink; g.font = "13px system-ui, sans-serif"; g.fillText("S", X(2.8), Y(0) - 6);
    var r = run(NT);
    g.strokeStyle = gr; g.globalAlpha = 0.55; g.lineWidth = 1;
    r.paths.forEach(function (pa) { g.beginPath(); pa.forEach(function (q, i) { var px = X(q[0]), py = Y(Math.max(-2.6, Math.min(2.6, q[1]))); if (i) g.lineTo(px, py); else g.moveTo(px, py); }); g.stroke(); });
    g.globalAlpha = 1; g.fillStyle = c1;
    r.paths.forEach(function (pa) { var q = pa[pa.length - 1]; g.beginPath(); g.arc(X(q[0]), Y(Math.max(-2.6, Math.min(2.6, q[1]))), 3.5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); g.fill(); });
    // bottom panel: histogram and target density
    var b0 = top + 8, bh = H - b0 - 18, nb = 60, hist = new Array(nb).fill(0);
    r.fin.forEach(function (x) { var k = Math.floor((x + 3) / 6 * nb); if (k >= 0 && k < nb) hist[k]++; });
    var dens = function (x) { var v = 0; M.forEach(function (m) { v += 0.5 * Math.exp(-(x - m) * (x - m) / (2 * s * s)) / (s * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)); }); return v; };
    var ymax = 1.3 * dens(M[0]), bw = 6 / nb;
    g.fillStyle = c1; g.globalAlpha = 0.75;
    hist.forEach(function (c, k) { var d = c / (NP * bw), hh = Math.min(d / ymax, 1) * bh; g.fillRect(X(-3 + k * bw) + 1, b0 + bh - hh, W / nb - 2, hh); });
    g.globalAlpha = 1; g.strokeStyle = ink; g.lineWidth = 2; g.beginPath();
    for (var i = 0; i <= 300; i++) { var x = -3 + 6 * i / 300, py = b0 + bh - dens(x) / ymax * bh; if (i) g.lineTo(X(x), py); else g.moveTo(X(x), py); }
    g.stroke();
    g.strokeStyle = hair; g.lineWidth = 1; g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(0, b0 + bh); g.lineTo(W, b0 + bh); g.stroke();
    g.fillStyle = ink; g.textAlign = "right"; g.fillText("target distribution on S", W - 8, b0 + 14); g.textAlign = "left";
    out.innerHTML = "<table><tr><td>mean final orthogonal component |y(1)|</td><td>" + f3(r.y) + (mode.value === "finale" ? " (before projection: " + f3(r.ybefore) + ")" : "") + "</td></tr>" +
      "<tr><td>error on the distribution in S, W₁(final positions, target)</td><td>" + f3(r.w1) + "</td></tr></table>";
  }
  [mode, tau, kap, nst].forEach(function (el) { el.addEventListener("input", draw); el.addEventListener("change", draw); });
  window.addEventListener("resize", draw);
  new MutationObserver(draw).observe(document.documentElement, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ["data-theme"] });
  if (window.matchMedia) { var mq = window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"); if (mq.addEventListener) mq.addEventListener("change", draw); }
  draw();
})();
</script>
```

With $\tau = 0$ and $\kappa = 0$, one checks Corollary 3.3: the final orthogonal component vanishes to machine precision (Proposition 3.4 with $\mathbf{e} = 0$), and the error on the distribution in $S$ only reflects the sampling error (2000 particles) and the Euler scheme. The truncation $\tau > 0$ leaves a final orthogonal component: this is the “divergence” of a free generation. The leakage $\kappa > 0$ distorts the distribution **within** $S$; the final projection cancels the divergence but not this distortion, whereas the projected flow, which keeps $y = 0$, removes it in this example.

### 3.4 Published work

Several recent works impose a hard constraint during sampling. They differ in the object being projected (the noisy state, the endpoint prediction, or both) and in the class of constraints they handle.

**Projected diffusion models** (Christopher, Baek and Fioretto 2024) project the state onto the feasible set $\mathcal{C}$ after each Langevin step: $\mathbf{x} \leftarrow P_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbf{x} + \gamma\,\mathbf{g} + \sqrt{2\gamma}\,\boldsymbol\epsilon)$. For a convex set, the feasibility of the samples is guaranteed; for a non-convex set, the authors use a projection initialized in the interior, without a formal guarantee. The cost per sample increases, moderately on some tasks (26.89 s against 18.51 s on their materials example) and strongly on others (682.40 s against 13.79 s for human motion).

**PCDM** (Li, Buzzicotti, Bonaccorso and Biferale 2026, preprint) generates rotating 3D turbulence ($64^3$, obtained by Galerkin truncation of $256^3$ simulations, Rossby number $Ro \approx 0.1$). The Leray projection is applied in Fourier space to the **clean estimate** produced by the network, and the noise used for the next step is recomputed from the projected estimate; the noisy state itself does not have to be solenoidal. The authors report a divergence that vanishes to machine precision and a training about five times shorter than their reference model (eight hundred thousand iterations, about 12 days, against four million, about 56 days). This is the closest 3D analogue of what the internship requires for $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0$ and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$.

**ECI** (Cheng, Han, Maddix, Ansari, Stuart, Mahoney and Wang 2025) handles, without any gradient computation, value constraints (initial and boundary conditions) and integral conservation laws on a functional flow matching model. Each step chains an **e**xtrapolation towards the end of the path, $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1 = \mathbf{u}_t + (1-t)v_\theta(\mathbf{u}_t)$, an exact **c**orrection of $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1$, and an **i**nterpolation back to $t'$: $\mathbf{u}_{t'} = (1-t')\mathbf{u}_0 + t'\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1$. The constraint is satisfied exactly if the correction is; on a Stokes problem, the authors measure 0.065 s per sample against 28.774 s for D-Flow (Ben-Hamu et al. 2024), a method that optimizes the initial noise by backpropagating through the whole flow.

**PCFM** (Utkarsh, Cai, Edelman, Gómez-Bombarelli and Rackauckas 2025) extends the idea to **nonlinear** constraints $h(\mathbf{u}) = 0$ (class C2): shooting towards the end of the path, Gauss–Newton projection $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{proj}} = \mathbf{u}_1 - J^{\mathsf{T}}(JJ^{\mathsf{T}})^{-1}h(\mathbf{u}_1)$ with $J$ the Jacobian of $h$, return through the interpolant, a few relaxed correction steps, and an exact final projection by Newton's method. The constraint is satisfied to machine precision, and the final projection accounts for 1 to 3% of the total time according to the authors.

**Genuist, Savin, Gatti and Clouteau (2026, preprint)** compare, on the same diffusion model for 2D periodic flows, a Leray projection applied to the noise, the state and the denoiser (variant “M”), a projection at the output of the denoiser (“D”), a progressive projection (“PC”), an a posteriori projection per frame (“SC”), and a soft penalty (“L”); we come back to it in Chapter 4.

Finally, **Neural conservation laws** (Richter-Powell, Lipman and Chen 2022) belongs to the architecture approach (Chapter 2): the constraint is satisfied by construction, without projection.

| Method | What is projected | Constraint | Guarantee | Reported cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Projected diffusion models | state after each Langevin step | convex set (or not) | exact if convex | ×1.4 to ×50 depending on the task |
| PCDM | clean estimate (Leray in Fourier space) | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0$ in 3D | machine precision | training ≈ 5 times shorter |
| Genuist et al., “M” | noise, state and denoiser | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0$ in 2D | machine precision | not quantified (spectral projection at each step) |
| ECI | extrapolated endpoint | values, integral conservation | exact if the correction is | 0.065 s against 28.774 s (D-Flow) |
| PCFM | endpoint, Gauss–Newton | nonlinear $h(\mathbf{u}) = 0$ | machine precision | final projection: 1 to 3% of the time |

### 3.5 Experiment: five ways of obtaining a divergence-free 2D field

The following code compares, at equal training budget, six variants on 2D periodic fields represented in a truncated Fourier basis ($|k_x|, |k_y| \le 2$, that is, 48 coefficients for $\mathbf{u}$ and 24 for $\psi$). The data distribution is non-Gaussian: the overall amplitude is random. We measure the relative divergence $\|\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}\|/\|\nabla\mathbf{u}\|$ (exact by Parseval) and the error on the distribution of the energy $E = \frac12\langle|\mathbf{u}|^2\rangle$, through the Wasserstein distance $W_1$ divided by the mean energy.

```python
import numpy as np, torch
from scipy.stats import wasserstein_distance
torch.set_num_threads(1); torch.manual_seed(0); rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Periodic 2D fields on [0, 2pi)^2 in a truncated Fourier basis (|kx|, |ky| <= 2):
# u(x) = sum_k a_k cos(k.x) + b_k sin(k.x), k in a half-plane (12 vectors), a_k, b_k in R^2.
ks = np.array([(i, j) for i in range(-2, 3) for j in range(-2, 3) if i > 0 or (i == 0 and j > 0)], float)
nk, kn = len(ks), np.linalg.norm(ks, axis=1)
e = np.stack([ks[:, 1], -ks[:, 0]], 1) / kn[:, None]          # unit vector orthogonal to k
D = 4 * nk                                                     # 48 coefficients (order: cos/sin, k, component)
P = np.zeros((D, D)); C = np.zeros((D, 2 * nk))
for cs in range(2):
    for i in range(nk):
        j = 2 * (cs * nk + i)
        P[j:j + 2, j:j + 2] = np.outer(e[i], e[i])             # Leray: I - k k^T / |k|^2
        C[j:j + 2, (1 - cs) * nk + i] = (1 if cs == 0 else -1) * kn[i] * e[i]   # u = grad^perp psi
K4 = np.concatenate([ks, ks])                                  # wave vector of each block (cos then sin)

def div_rel(x):          # ||div u||_L2 / ||grad u||_L2, exact by Parseval
    c = x.reshape(len(x), 2 * nk, 2)
    return np.sqrt(((c * K4).sum(-1)**2).sum(1) / ((c**2).sum(-1) * (K4**2).sum(-1)).sum(1))

def donnees(N):          # non-Gaussian distribution: random amplitude r ~ U(0.5, 1.5), psi spectrum in |k|^-2
    r = rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5, (N, 1))
    psi = r * np.tile(kn, 2) ** -2.0 * rng.normal(size=(N, 2 * nk))
    return psi @ C.T, psi                                      # (u, psi)

def entraine(X, penalite=0.0, bruit_dans_S=False, steps=1000):
    X = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32); d = X.shape[1]
    Pt = torch.tensor(P, dtype=torch.float32); Q = torch.eye(D) - Pt
    net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(d + 1, 128), torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(128, 128),
                              torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(128, d))
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        x1 = X[torch.randint(len(X), (256,))]; x0 = torch.randn_like(x1); t = torch.rand(256, 1)
        if bruit_dans_S: x0 = x0 @ Pt.T                        # Gaussian noise supported on S
        xt = (1 - t) * x0 + t * x1
        v = net(torch.cat([xt, t], 1))
        loss = ((v - (x1 - x0))**2).sum(1).mean()
        if penalite:     # soft penalty on the endpoint prediction  x1_hat = xt + (1 - t) v
            loss = loss + penalite * (((xt + (1 - t) * v) @ Q.T)**2).sum(1).mean()
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return net

@torch.no_grad()
def genere(net, x0, proj=None, n=50):
    x = torch.tensor(x0, dtype=torch.float32)
    Pt = None if proj is None else torch.tensor(proj, dtype=torch.float32)
    if Pt is not None: x = x @ Pt.T
    for i in range(n):
        x = x + net(torch.cat([x, torch.full((len(x), 1), i / n)], 1)) / n
        if Pt is not None: x = x @ Pt.T                       # projected flow: reproject at each step
    return x.double().numpy()

U, Psi = donnees(4000); Uref, _ = donnees(2000)
# Normalization: one factor per block (cos or sin, k), shared by the 2 components, so P is unchanged;
# it brings the component in S to unit variance, like that of the noise.
su = np.repeat(np.sqrt((U.reshape(-1, 2 * nk, 2)**2).sum(2).mean(0)), 2); sp = Psi.std(0)
E = lambda x: 0.25 * (x**2).sum(1)                             # energy (1/2)<|u|^2> by Parseval
print(f"data             : mean E = {E(U).mean():.2f}, median div_rel = {np.median(div_rel(U)):.1e}, "
      f"W1(E)/E floor = {wasserstein_distance(E(donnees(2000)[0]), E(Uref)) / E(Uref).mean():.3f}")
z = rng.normal(size=(2000, D))
net_u, net_pen = entraine(U / su), entraine(U / su, penalite=1.0)
net_S, net_psi = entraine(U / su, bruit_dans_S=True), entraine(Psi / sp)
res = {"free": genere(net_u, z) * su}
res["final projection"] = res["free"] @ P.T
res["projected flow"] = genere(net_u, z, proj=P) * su
res["soft penalty"] = genere(net_pen, z) * su
res["flow in S"] = genere(net_S, z, proj=P) * su              # projected noise during training AND at sampling
res["potential psi"] = (genere(net_psi, z[:, :2 * nk]) * sp) @ C.T
for nom, x in res.items():
    print(f"{nom:17s}: median div_rel = {np.median(div_rel(x)):.1e}, W1(E)/E = {wasserstein_distance(E(x), E(Uref)) / E(Uref).mean():.3f}")
# output:
# data             : mean E = 2.42, median div_rel = 0.0e+00, W1(E)/E floor = 0.020
# free             : median div_rel = 7.1e-02, W1(E)/E = 0.654
# final projection : median div_rel = 0.0e+00, W1(E)/E = 0.645
# projected flow   : median div_rel = 0.0e+00, W1(E)/E = 0.724
# soft penalty     : median div_rel = 7.7e-02, W1(E)/E = 0.559
# flow in S        : median div_rel = 0.0e+00, W1(E)/E = 0.178
# potential psi    : median div_rel = 0.0e+00, W1(E)/E = 0.154
```

![Result of the code block above (measured on this page, one seed, 1000 training iterations per model). Bars: relative error on the distribution of the energy, $W_1(E)/\langle E\rangle$; the dotted line is the floor due to sampling (two draws from the true distribution). Right: median relative divergence. In blue, the mechanisms that make the divergence vanish to machine precision; in gray, those that do not. With a second seed, the values move by a few hundredths and the ranking is the same, except that the flow in $S$ and the potential, which are very close, swap places (0.195 and 0.203).](../../../prep/p8-contraintes-physiques/fig-mecanismes-divergence-en.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart. Free: 0.65 and divergence 7.1·10⁻²; soft penalty: 0.56 and 7.7·10⁻²; free plus final projection: 0.65, zero divergence; projected flow: 0.72, zero divergence; flow in S: 0.18, zero divergence; potential psi: 0.15, zero divergence. Sampling floor at 0.02."}

Four observations, to be read as observations on a small example and not as general laws. (1) The four exact mechanisms cancel the divergence, here exactly (zero on all 2000 samples): the components of $\mathbf{k}$ are $0$, $\pm1$ or $\pm2$, so the ratios between the coefficients involved are powers of 2 and the rounding errors cancel exactly; in general, one obtains machine precision (of order $10^{-7}$ in single precision). (2) The soft penalty does not reduce the divergence: Proposition 4.3 will explain why. (3) The final projection cancels the divergence of free generation without improving the distribution of the energy: it corrects what lies outside $S$, not what lies in $S$. (4) At equal budget, the two variants that never ask the network to learn the stiff orthogonal component (flow in $S$ and potential) are clearly better than the others, and close to each other, as predicted by Corollary 3.3 (b); the projected flow, which evaluates a network trained with a full noise on inputs without an orthogonal component, is the worst. In the limit of perfect learning, all variants would give the same distribution: the gap measures the cost of learning a useless term.

The internship compares these mechanisms on forced 2D MHD fields conditioned on the diffusivity $\eta$, with a real convolutional network and five variants (free, penalty, final projection, projected flow, potentials): the results are in the [report, experiment E2](../../rapport/index.html#e2).

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 3
:::
- If $\mu(S) = 1$ and the noise is isotropic Gaussian, $v^\star = v_S(P\mathbf{x}, t) - (I - P)\mathbf{x}/(1 - t)$: the component in $S$ does not see the orthogonal component, which is an explicit and stiff restoring term.
- With $v^\star$, free generation, final projection, projected flow, flow in $S$ and potentials give the same distribution; the practical differences come from the learning.
- With Euler, the final divergence of a free generation is exactly $h$ times the orthogonal error of the network at the last step.
- Projecting at the end corrects the constraint, not the distribution in $S$; training with a noise supported on $S$ (or generating potentials) avoids learning the stiff term.
- Published: projected diffusion (convex, guaranteed), PCDM (Leray on the estimate, 3D), ECI (gradient-free, value constraints), PCFM (nonlinear, Gauss–Newton).
::::

## 4. Soft constraints: penalties {#ch4}

A constraint that one cannot make exact by construction or by projection (a complex stationary PDE residual, an inequality constraint) can be added to the training loss, as in a physics-informed neural network (PINN). This is simple and generic, but the constraint is then only approximately satisfied, and the way it is evaluated during the training of a generative model raises a specific difficulty: the Jensen gap.

### 4.1 Penalty on the endpoint prediction

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Penalized loss]{.tag}
For a constraint $c(\mathbf{x}) = 0$ that holds for every data point, one adds to the flow matching loss a term evaluated on the **endpoint prediction** $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1 = \mathbf{x}_t + (1-t)\,v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)$:

$$
\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{pen}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\big\|v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) - (\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0)\big\|^2 + \lambda\,\mathbb{E}\big[w(t)\,\|c(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1)\|^2\big],
$$

with a weight $\lambda > 0$ and a time weighting $w(t) \ge 0$.
:::

One penalizes $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1$ rather than $\mathbf{x}_t$ because $\mathbf{x}_t$ is noisy and satisfies no constraint; $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1$ is the network's estimate of the clean field towards which one is heading.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Unbiased penalty for a linear constraint, biased otherwise]{.tag}
At the optimal field, $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1 = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_1 \mid \mathbf{x}_t]$. If $c(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ is linear and $A\mathbf{x}_1 = 0$ almost surely, the penalty vanishes at $v^\star$: it does not move the optimum. If $c$ is nonlinear, in general $c(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_1\mid\mathbf{x}_t]) \neq \mathbb{E}[c(\mathbf{x}_1)\mid\mathbf{x}_t] = 0$: the penalty is nonzero at the optimum of flow matching and moves the optimum. The gap $c(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_1\mid\mathbf{x}_t]) - \mathbb{E}[c(\mathbf{x}_1)\mid\mathbf{x}_t]$ is called the **Jensen gap**.

::: proof
For $v^\star(\mathbf{x}, t) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0 \mid \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{x}]$, one has $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1 = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_t + (1-t)(\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0) \mid \mathbf{x}_t] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_1 \mid \mathbf{x}_t]$, since $\mathbf{x}_t + (1-t)(\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{x}_1$. If $c = A$ is linear, $A\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_1\mid\mathbf{x}_t] = \mathbb{E}[A\mathbf{x}_1\mid\mathbf{x}_t] = 0$, so the penalty vanishes at $v^\star$, which also minimizes the first term: $v^\star$ remains the minimizer of the sum. If $c$ is nonlinear, the expectation does not commute with $c$; Example 4.4 gives an explicit case where the gap is nonzero. The gradient of the penalty at $v^\star$ is then nonzero in general, and the optimum of $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{pen}}$ differs from $v^\star$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a linear constraint, the penalty is therefore harmless. But is it useful? The following proposition shows that it brings nothing new, and that it acts little where the divergence is decided.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — A linear penalty is a reweighting of the orthogonal loss]{.tag}
Under the assumptions of Proposition 3.2, with $c = I - P$ (the orthogonal component), the penalty of Definition 4.1 equals

$$
\big\|(I-P)\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1\big\|^2 = (1-t)^2\,\big\|(I-P)\big(v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) - v^\star(\mathbf{x}_t, t)\big)\big\|^2.
$$

It is the error of the network on the orthogonal component, weighted by $(1-t)^2$, which vanishes at $t = 1$.

::: proof
$(I-P)\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1 = (I-P)\mathbf{x}_t + (1-t)(I-P)v_\theta$. By Proposition 3.2, $(I-P)v^\star(\mathbf{x}_t, t) = -(I-P)\mathbf{x}_t/(1-t)$, hence $(I-P)\mathbf{x}_t = -(1-t)(I-P)v^\star$ and $(I-P)\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1 = (1-t)(I-P)(v_\theta - v^\star)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Proposition 3.4 showed that the final divergence is set by the orthogonal error of the network in the vicinity of $t = 1$. The penalty weights precisely this error by $(1-t)^2$, which is almost zero there: this is why, in the experiment of Section 3.5, the penalty does not reduce the divergence. A weighting $w(t) = (1-t)^{-2}$ would compensate for this factor, but it would only amount to multiplying by $1 + \lambda$ the weight of the orthogonal component in the flow matching loss, which already contains it (Exercise 7).

::: ex
[Example 4.4 — The Jensen gap on a circle]{.tag}
Take data uniform on the unit circle, with the nonlinear constraint $c(\mathbf{x}) = |\mathbf{x}|^2 - 1 = 0$. The posterior distribution of $\mathbf{x}_1$ given $\mathbf{x}_t$ is supported on the circle; its mean is a convex combination of points of the circle, hence **inside** the disk, and $c(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1) < 0$ strictly as long as the posterior distribution is not a Dirac. Exercise 8 gives the exact formula: $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1 = \frac{I_1(\kappa)}{I_0(\kappa)}\frac{\mathbf{x}_t}{|\mathbf{x}_t|}$ with $\kappa = t|\mathbf{x}_t|/(1-t)^2$, where $I_0, I_1$ are modified Bessel functions. A penalty $\|c(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1)\|^2$ would therefore push $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1$ towards the circle, that is, **away** from the true conditional expectation. For data on a line (linear constraint), the mean stays on the line.
:::

The following interactive diagram shows the Jensen gap as a function of the flow time.
